newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: YACHTING-MORNING GLORY RETAKES LEAD, HEADS FOR RACE RECORD.
newsitem.headline: YACHTING-MORNING GLORY RETAKES LEAD, HEADS FOR RACE RECORD.

text.p: German maxi Morning Glory regained the lead in the Sydney-to-Hobart overnight and was on schedule to break the 21-year race record on Saturday as she powered under spinnaker down the east coast of Tasmania.
At the morning race schedule the 24.5-metre (80-foot) maxi was five hours inside the record with only 212 nautical miles to the finish line at Hobart, the capital of Tasmania.
"Morning Glory is set to take the record at this stage," said a race official in Hobart.
"We have done a computer calculation and she is expected to cross the finish line around 10.20 p.m. tonight," she said.
Morning Glory must cross the finish line by 3.36 a.m. on Sunday to break the race record of two days, 14 hours 36 minutes and 56 seconds set by U.S. maxi ketch Kialoa in 1975.

In second place in the 630 nautical mile race was Hong Kong pocket maxi Exile, eight nautical miles astern of Morning Glory, with Australian maxi Amazon third a further two nautical miles behind. Overnight, four more boats retired damaged, reducing the original 95-boat fleet to 82.

Sailing under spinnaker on Saturday morning in a 30-knot northeasterly tailwind, Morning Glory had a boat speed of around 15 knots -- a speed which would easily put her across the finish line inside the race record. Ironically, Kialoa managed to only average 10 knots in her record breaking run to Hobart.
A 30-knot southerly headwind forecast for later in the day will slow Morning Glory, but she proved earlier in the race that she can make good speed under heavy headwinds.

A 40-knot southerly buster only hours into the race on Thursday saw many race favourites forced to retire with broken masts and shreaded sails. But Morning Glory, which was one of 25 boats forced to restart the race after jumping the gun, survived the battering conditions to take the lead on the first day.
The Sydney-to-Hobart race record has stood for 21 years mainly because of the unpredicatable winds off Tasmania's east coast and in the final run up the Derwent River to the finish.
In the past two years, the lead yacht has been well within the race record charging down the east coast of Tasmania, only to be becalmed and robbed of the record.
"The Derwent is where the race record will be determined. It is in a wind shadow and it will all depend on conditions when the boats arrive on the river," said a race official.
If Morning Glory does break the record, she will collect A$300,000 (US$237,000), the richest prizemoney for a record-breaking line-honours win in a single ocean race.
